items.title: What Should SFT Learn? Conditional Information Gain for Generalizable Post-Training
items.content: arXiv:2610.12995v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) remains a widely used approach for post-training large language models, because fixed demonstrations can directly introduce desired reasoning strategies and behavioral patterns. Yet forcing a model to imitate externally provided trajectories may also interfere with behaviors already supported by pretraining, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. Recent dynamic SFT methods mitigate this issue by reweighting token-level supervision according to model-side signals such as predictive probability, prior support, or distributional compatibility. However, model compatibility is not equivalent to learning value: a token that is weakly supported by the current model may either be an undesirable mismatch or precisely the task-specific decision that the demonstration is intended to teach. We propose CIG-SFT, an information-theoretic framework that estimates the task-conditioned information carried by each demonstrated token. Under teacher forcing, we compare the token likelihood from a frozen reference model with and without access to the task input while keeping the gold solution prefix fixed. The resulting conditional information gain quantifies how much the task itself reduces uncertainty about the demonstrated decision. We then convert this information into a KL-regularized projection of the current policy and derive an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective whose logit gradient exactly matches that of the projected target. Across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, CIG-SFT consistently outperforms standard SFT and recent adaptive fine-tuning baselines, with particularly strong improvements in generalization to challenging evaluation distributions, while requiring neither additional training data nor online rollouts.

items.summary: The paper argues that model-compatibility signals used in dynamic supervised fine-tuning (token probability, prior support) conflate compatibility with learning value, and that forcing imitation can interfere with behaviors already supported by pretraining. It proposes conditional information gain as a token-weighting criterion for SFT that better targets generalizable post-training. This refines a growing line of work on selective token-level supervision.

Impact depends on empirical generality across tasks, which the abstract does not fully establish.

items.title: PRIME: Pre-Retrieval Index Modeling Enhancement for Structured Document Retrieval-Real
items.content: arXiv:2610.13296v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: High-precision retrieval over external knowledge bases is essential for LLM agents to operate effectively. However, existing Information Retrieval (IR) research primarily optimizes query-side retrievers (e.g., ColBERT, BGE) and generators (e.g., Self-RAG, GraphRAG), while reducing corpus-side representation to chunking. This leaves index-side quality an underexplored lever. We propose Pre-Retrieval Index Modeling & Enhancement (PRIME), an index-side optimization framework built on two complementary tracks: an LLM-driven Semantic Restructuring (SR) track that transforms long documents into structured, information-dense sections, and a deterministic Metadata Synthesis (MS) and Hierarchical Retrieval (HR) track that extracts semantic anchors and heading structure for coarse-to-fine section retrieval. Our evaluations show that deterministic metadata matches structure-aware chunking's retrieval quality while cutting embedding computation by 45.8 $\times$ and index vector count by 22.4 $\times$. On top of these gains, Semantic Restructuring (SR) further improves Answer-F1 by 13.7% in full deployment, with characterized quality-fidelity-cost trade-offs. Across QASPER, BRIGHT, and NFCorpus, we further characterize three qualitative regimes that determine whether index-side optimization helps or degrades retrieval, while showing that these index-side effects are neutralized under a strong reranker.

items.summary: PRIME is an index-side optimization framework for retrieval-augmented LLM agents that complements the usual query-side focus. It combines an LLM-driven semantic restructuring track that converts long documents into information-dense sections with deterministic metadata synthesis and hierarchical retrieval to create semantic anchors. This addresses an underexplored lever in RAG pipelines: corpus/index quality rather than retriever or generator improvements.

items.title: When Edge Independence Fails: Joint Graph Diffusion with Latent Sociability Priors
items.content: arXiv:2610.13765v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Discrete graph diffusion models corrupt graph structure through independent edge updates with a Markovian noise model. Combined with the exchangeability requirement on the output distribution, the terminal prior is necessarily an Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi (E-R) random graph. This has a fundamental consequence for unconditional graph generation without node features: in the large graph limit, any GNN denoiser applied to an E-R graph approximately outputs an E-R graph, making effective denoising difficult. In practice, generated graphs fail to recover meaningful node heterogeneity and higher-order structure. Previous models introduced specialized node features to compensate, framing this as an expressivity problem, while the role of the prior remained unexamined. We instead address the root cause by introducing the Latent Sociability Prior (LSP) and a join} diffusion process that co-evolves latent node sociability variables and graph structure, removing edge independence while preserving exchangeability. Unlike existing latent graph diffusion methods, the sociability mechanism requires no complex encoder: its sole role is to guide edge updates and preserve node heterogeneity throughout the trajectory. We validate our approach on multiple graph generation datasets and show that the proposed framework more accurately captures graph distributions than baseline methods without node features.

The work provides theoretical grounding for why unconditional featureless graph generation has struggled in practice.

items.title: A Categorical Atlas of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: Cones, Orbits, and Gauges
items.content: arXiv:2610.12728v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning has hundreds of methods, usually compared by parameter count and benchmark score. We compare them as maps. A pretrained checkpoint is a base point in weight space, and a weight-space method is a smooth map from a small parameter space that starts at that point. These maps form a slice category in which the frozen model is initial and full fine-tuning terminal. Three invariants of the map do most of the work. Its image near the base point governs expressivity, through the first-order image, the dimension, a min-cut bound on rank and whether that point is smooth or an apex. Its fibres, with the optimizer's metric, govern training dynamics. Base change moves the base point and covers splitting initialisations, quantisation, restarts and merging. We prove, for example, that zero-initialised LoRA, and Householder reflection adaptation at its default start under stated rank and parity conditions, begin at the apex of a cone; that no exact initialisation lets LoRA reach an update of rank above twice its own; that exactly orthogonal methods never change a weight's singular values in exact arithmetic, however often they are merged; that under Adam with no epsilon, weight decay or clipping and one shared schedule, LoRA+ from the standard zero initialisation follows exactly the trajectory of plain LoRA with its scale multiplied by the learning-rate ratio; that Adam with shared hyperparameters respects only the signed permutations inside LoRA's continuous symmetry group of full-rank factors; and that the activation function decides when a scaling adapter folds into preceding weights. We classify 382 methods from 138 papers by seven coordinates read off their formulas, with 403 simulation arrows and 485 obstructions. Every numbered result is proved in full, and results due to others are credited where we re-derive them.

Three invariants of these maps (local image, fibers, base change) organize expressivity, training dynamics, and common PEFT design moves.

items.title: Controlled-Minimax: Stabilizing Adversarial Optimization via Control Theory
items.content: arXiv:2610.12915v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Minimax optimization is fundamental to adversarial learning yet suffers from severe stability challenges, often manifesting as persistent limit cycles or divergence. This paper investigates these instabilities through the lens of continuous-time dynamical systems. By modeling training dynamics as a second-order Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE), we rigorously identify the root cause of non-convergence: the problematic eigenstructure of the loss function's Hessian near equilibrium points. To address this, we introduce Controlled-Minimax, a novel stabilization framework that reformulates the optimization trajectory as a controllable physical system. Unlike heuristic regularization techniques, our approach derives a specific feedback controller that provides theoretical guarantees of local exponential stability, regardless of the underlying Hessian spectrum. Consequently, our method stabilizes general minimax problems where traditional gradient descent-ascent methods fail. Extensive experiments on pathological benchmarks including the Dirac-GAN, 2D Gaussian mixtures, and Swiss Roll datasets, as well as high-resolution image synthesis with StyleGAN2-ada, demonstrate that Controlled-Minimax effectively suppresses oscillatory behavior while ensuring fast and robust convergence.

It proposes Controlled-Minimax, which treats the optimization trajectory as a controllable physical system and applies derived feedback control rather than heuristic regularization. This offers a principled remedy for limit cycles and divergence in adversarial learning.

items.title: CAST: Credit Alignment for Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2610.13257v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation (OPD) requires aligning teacher and student sequences before their scores can be compared. Decoded-text alignment provides such correspondence at the chunk level, but leaves a distinct problem unresolved: credit alignment. A chunk-level signal specifies how much a span should change, but not how that signal should be distributed across student tokens, while tokens without teacher correspondence remain unconstrained. We propose CAST (Chunk-aware credit Assignment with Selective Token Anchoring), a shift-or-stay framework that addresses both issues. For aligned chunks, CAST redistributes each chunk's advantage across student tokens using predictive uncertainty and local teacher-signal smoothness, emphasizing learning opportunities supported by locally consistent teacher feedback while preserving the chunk's total advantage. The resulting weights exactly solve a KL-regularized credit-allocation problem. For unaligned positions, CAST selectively anchors the student to its initial policy through a KL penalty, limiting drift where teacher supervision is unavailable. Because credit assignment is separated from chunk construction, CAST also applies to punctuation-defined or fixed-length chunks under shared tokenization. Across six mathematics, science, and code benchmarks, CAST improves the average over the strongest evaluated baseline by $2.45$ and $1.32$ points for cross-tokenizer transfer from Qwen3-8B to Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively, and by $2.10$ points for shared-tokenizer transfer to Qwen3-1.7B.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.13257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation (OPD) requires aligning teacher and student sequences before their scores can be compared. Decoded-text alignment provides such correspondence at the chunk level, but leaves a distinct problem unresolved: credit alignment. A chunk-level signal specifies how much a span should change, but not how that signal should be distributed across student tokens, while tokens without teacher correspondence remain unconstrained. We propose CAST (Chunk-aware credit Assignment with Selective Token Anchoring), a shift-or-stay framework that addresses both issues. For aligned chunks, CAST redistributes each chunk's advantage across student tokens using predictive uncertainty and local teacher-signal smoothness, emphasizing learning opportunities supported by locally consistent teacher feedback while preserving the chunk's total advantage. The resulting weights exactly solve a KL-regularized credit-allocation problem. For unaligned positions, CAST selectively anchors the student to its initial policy through a KL penalty, limiting drift where teacher supervision is unavailable. Because credit assignment is separated from chunk construction, CAST also applies to punctuation-defined or fixed-length chunks under shared tokenization. Across six mathematics, science, and code benchmarks, CAST improves the average over the strongest evaluated baseline by $2.45$ and $1.32$ points for cross-tokenizer transfer from Qwen3-8B to Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively, and by $2.10$ points for shared-tokenizer transfer to Qwen3-1.7B.

items.title: CopRoute: Dependence-Aware Conformal Routing for Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.13276v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Set-based language model routing aims to increase the coverage of the event where at least one model answers a query correctly while controlling the number of inference calls made. Existing risk-controlled routing policies bound the all-miss risk (the probability that every model in the selected set fails) by calibrating a single conformal threshold and applying it to a nested family of model sets. Because each model is scored in isolation, these policies ignore the dependence structure of model failures. Models that share training data or architecture tend to fail on the same queries, so two individually strong models can be jointly redundant while a weaker but complementary model covers the queries that the others miss. To account for this dependence, which existing risk-controlled policies ignore, we propose CopRoute, which orders models by how many new queries each one answers correctly beyond those already selected, decides per query how far down that order to go, and then picks the smallest cutoff that still meets the target risk. We show that CopRoute's ordering attains, on the design data, the best guarantee any efficient fixed-ordering algorithm can give for the average number of calls to the first correct model, and that a separate calibration step certifies the all-miss risk of the deployed sets. On RouterBench and RouterEval, CopRoute attains the fewest certified calls on nine of ten datasets at a target risk of 0.05 and on eight of ten at 0.10, making up to 79 percent fewer calls (median 24 percent) than the state-of-the-art risk-controlled policy at the same certified all-miss risk.
items.author: Siva Rajesh Kasa, Santhosh Kumar Kasa, Karan Gupta
items.summary: Introduces a conformal routing method for set-based LLM routing that accounts for the dependence structure of model failures, unlike prior risk-controlled policies that score models in isolation with a single threshold. By exploiting complementarity between models, it can control all-miss risk while reducing redundant inference calls. Relevant to cost-efficient multi-model serving.
items.reasoning: Addresses a practically important gap in conformal routing by modeling failure correlation among models with shared training data or architectures; solid methodological contribution, though niche and evaluated presumably on moderate-scale setups.

items.title: SBNO : Schr\"odinger Bridge Neural Operator for the Forward and Inverse Problems under Missing Information
items.content: arXiv:2610.13317v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE) surrogate modeling often relies on either dense observations or access to governing equations/physics constraints. In practice, observations can be sparse and partial, and the underlying physics may be partially specified or unavailable. We introduce SBNO, an equation-free paired-data diffusion bridge matching framework that learns conditional operators for both forward and inverse PDE problems under partial observations. SBNO uses diffusion Schr\"odinger bridge matching to learn a pair of time-dependent drifts from a mask-aware endpoint coupling that preserves empirical input-solution pairing during training and supports both PDE-task directions within a single framework. At inference time, SBNO produces a deterministic point reconstruction by integrating the probability-flow ODE constructed from the learned drift pair, without inference-time observation or PDE guidance-weight tuning. On five PDE benchmarks with 5% observations, SBNO achieves superior or comparable accuracy to baselines while demonstrating lower test-instance error dispersion. Furthermore, SBNO is at least $9.7 \times$ faster and reduces GPU memory by at least $4.3 \times$ compared to guided-diffusion baselines.

This matters because practical scientific applications often lack the dense data or fully specified equations that conventional neural operators require.

items.title: Studying the Effects of Task Diversity Using Small Mathematical Worlds
items.content: arXiv:2610.13750v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Basic mathematical tasks like modular addition have been a valuable tool for illuminating aspects of neural network behavior that are challenging to see in noisy, unverifiable, large-scale, real-world settings. These studies have typically focused on a single task. However, modern language models are exposed to a vast number of tasks despite being trained with a next-token prediction objective. In this work, we introduce two mathematical task ecosystems, IntWorld and PermWorld, built from distinct but related tasks on integers and permutations. Both are designed to simulate task diversity within a cohesive mathematical 'world' where tasks are distinct but related. Because the datasets are procedurally generated, we can precisely vary the number of tasks, allowing us to begin to disentangle the role of task variety from other factors in training. After describing the datasets, we provide some initial results obtained from these datasets which support the idea that increasing task diversity increases the richness of a model's internal representations.
items.author: Emily Xia Meng, Xuanyu Yang, Junaid Hasan, Michael Ruofan Zeng, Henry Kvinge
items.summary: The authors introduce IntWorld and PermWorld, procedurally generated ecosystems of distinct but related mathematical tasks that permit precise control of task diversity. These small worlds serve as tractable testbeds for studying how task diversity during training shapes neural network behavior, mimicking the multi-task exposure of language models.
items.reasoning: A useful methodological contribution to the growing small-math-worlds research program; controllable task diversity testbeds can yield mechanistic insights, but findings are preliminary by design.

items.title: Prediction Is Not a Sufficient Memory State
items.content: arXiv:2610.13881v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A memory that reproduces every current prediction may still have forgotten how to learn from the next observation. We characterize this distinction for exact cumulative learning and attention. For smooth convex residual losses with unrestricted real features and labels, a continuous recurrent state of fixed dimension exists exactly when the loss is polynomial. With ordinary, unweighted observations, degree $D$ requires precisely $r=\binom{d+D}{D}-1$ coordinates; even among histories with one fixed current predictor, exactly $r-d$ coordinates can remain necessary for continuation. Nonpolynomial losses have unbounded requirements on such equal-prediction histories. Bounded scalar logistic examples retain this obstruction after fixing any finite derivative jet. For ridge regression, the hidden evidence is the design matrix: the exact state costs $dp+d(d+1)/2$, versus $dp$ for the predictor. On a well-conditioned zero-prediction family, optimal $B$-bit compression has average one-update error of order $d^{-1}2^{-2B/s_d}$, $s_d=d(d+1)/2$, even with arbitrary randomized codes. Kernel attention gives a second exact closure classification. The results identify what future updates reveal, rather than proposing a new regression algorithm or asserting trained-model gains.
items.author: Robert Jenkinson Alvarez
items.summary: This theory paper characterizes when a fixed-dimension recurrent state can support exact cumulative learning, proving that for smooth convex residual losses such a state exists exactly when the loss is polynomial, with precise coordinate requirements growing combinatorially in degree. Non-polynomial losses yield unbounded memory requirements even among histories with identical current predictions.
items.reasoning: Rigorous and conceptually striking theoretical result distinguishing prediction competence from the capacity to keep learning, with implications for understanding memory in recurrent models and attention; single-author and highly abstract, so practical reach is uncertain.

items.title: MolP2SBench: Do LLMs Really Reason from Molecular Properties to Structure?
items.content: arXiv:2610.12522v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in molecular discovery and structure elucidation, where decisions depend on physical observations. Existing evaluations primarily focus on end-to-end molecular reconstruction, where correct predictions do not necessarily indicate reliance on the supplied properties. We introduce MolP2SBench, a benchmark for molecular property-to-structure (P2S) reasoning in LLMs. Each task presents a masked molecular scaffold with given properties and asks the model to select the missing structure from plausible candidates. We shuffle or replace properties to test reliance on correct property-structure pairing and responsiveness to counterfactual property changes. A channel-wise leaderboard uses Property-Grounded Recovery (PGR), giving equal weight to source and counterfactual recovery. Evaluating seven models, we find that LLMs can use physical properties for structure prediction, but performance varies substantially across property types. Higher accuracy with a property does not necessarily imply greater responsiveness to it: a model may benefit more from $^1$H NMR than from $^{13}$C NMR, yet be less likely to change its prediction when the $^1$H data is replaced. LLM performance also need not reflect the relative difficulty of these properties for human chemists. Although UV-Vis spectra provide less direct structural information than NMR spectra, Astra achieves higher accuracy with UV-Vis data than with NMR peaks. MolP2SBench supports studying how LLMs extract and use physical-property information, revealing patterns that may differ from conventional chemical intuition and providing a foundation for more reliably property-grounded models for molecular and quantum-chemical inference. Code and dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/MolP2SBench.

items.title: Two-way Guidance: Simultaneous Learning of Summary Statistics for Generative Bayes
items.content: arXiv:2610.12850v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) can struggle to recover increasingly concentrated posteriors as observation size grows. We consider learning sufficient summary statistics jointly with the posterior as a general principle for scalable inference in various SBI methods. A common measure taken in SBI is dimension reduction through predetermined summaries, which may partially discard posterior information. Our approach instead imposes structure on how the posterior learner depends on a learned summary (e.g., affinity), and learns the summary simultaneously with the posterior. We identify an important mechanism named two-way guidance: under a structural restriction on the summary, the posterior sufficiency of the learned summary simplifies posterior learning, whereas a suitable posterior objective guides the learned summary towards posterior sufficiency. This mechanism explains a counterintuitive finding that the structural restriction on the summary statistics improves posterior learning, rather than limit its performance. We establish theoretical guarantees on both posterior estimation error and the learned summary's departure from sufficiency, thus identifying conditions on the simulation budget for recovering increasingly concentrated posteriors as observation size grows.

The identified two-way guidance mechanism helps scalable SBI recover concentrated posteriors as observation size grows.
items.reasoning: A principled general framework for a known weakness of SBI with broad applicability across SBI methods, though it is a niche statistical methodology without headline empirical results.

items.title: Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion Generation from Spatial Audio
items.content: arXiv:2610.13300v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Modeling human reactions to spatial audio requires understanding both what is heard and where it comes from. Prior work generates motion offline from complete acoustic and spatial input sequences. Humans, however, react to sounds without knowing what they will hear next. We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from spatial audio. The model encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens. Conditioned on these tokens, a causal transformer with a flow head generates continuous motion latents, from which a causal decoder reconstructs motion segments. Standard teacher-forced training derives motion histories and body-relative source locations from ground-truth motion, whereas streaming inference relies on generated motion for both, resulting in a training-inference mismatch. To reduce this history discrepancy, we introduce rehearsal training, which combines full-sequence teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction along short autoregressive self-rollouts. To keep spatial conditioning consistent with generated motion, we propose spatial feedback, which recomputes body-relative source locations from generated root poses during both rehearsal training and inference. On SAM, Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision. It further supports real-time online generation of coherent reactions across sound events and source locations. Project page: https://jingchengni.com/sonic-amg/.
items.author: Jingcheng Ni, Zekun Li, Zhiyang Dou, Xiaoyan Cong, Ziyao Zeng, Hongyang Du, Randall Balestriero, Taku Komura, Srinath Sridhar
items.summary: Sonic-AMG is presented as the first framework for streaming human motion generation conditioned on spatial audio, encoding acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens for a causal transformer with a flow head. Unlike prior offline approaches, the model reacts to sounds as they arrive, mimicking human reactive behavior. This enables applications in VR, avatars, and interactive agents.

items.title: Asymptotic Analysis of Discrete-Time Self-Attention Dynamics in Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2610.13518v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In machine learning, a self-attention dynamics describes the attention mechanism of transformers, and is obtained treating the layer index of a transformer as time index. Even though naturally discrete-time, this dynamical system is most often studied in continuous-time. Scope of this paper is to provide a thorough investigation of the discrete-time version of the self-attention dynamics: a complete classification of its equilibria is given, and their stability properties are studied, in both the single-head and the multihead case. We show that in both cases the main attractor of the dynamics is a consensus equilibrium aligned with the principal eigenvector of the value matrix (in the single-head case, a corresponding matrix of weights in the multihead case), even though other locally asymptotically stable bipartite equilibria can be show to exist at least in the single-head situation. The behavior is confirmed by looking at the learned weight matrices of a real transformer.
items.author: Claudio Altafini
items.summary: The paper provides a thorough discrete-time analysis of self-attention dynamics, giving a complete classification of equilibria and their stability in single-head and multihead cases, in contrast to prior continuous-time treatments. It shows the main attractor is a consensus equilibrium aligned with the principal eigenvector of the value matrix. This deepens theoretical understanding of how transformers' attention layers evolve when layer index is treated as time.

items.title: Scalable Sparse Autoregressive Variational Inference for Non-Gaussian Spatial Fields
items.content: arXiv:2610.13656v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Latent field models are essential for spatial statistics, but the posterior distribution of the latent field, even with a Gaussian process (GP) prior, is analytically intractable whenever the likelihood is non-Gaussian. Existing approximations are either too slow or too restrictive for large non-Gaussian datasets. We present a scalable variational inference framework that mirrors the sparse nearest-neighbor autoregressive structure of the prior in the variational family, uses normalizing-flow conditionals for expressiveness, and amortizes all variational parameters via a single shared neural conditioner. Doubly stochastic optimization with reduced ancestor sets achieves polylogarithmic complexity per iteration.
items.author: Paul F. V. Wiemann, Matthias Katzfuss
items.summary: This work introduces a scalable variational inference framework for latent Gaussian process models with non-Gaussian likelihoods, mirroring the sparse nearest-neighbor autoregressive structure of the prior in the variational family. It uses normalizing-flow conditionals and a shared neural conditioner to amortize parameters, achieving polylogarithmic per-iteration complexity on large spatial datasets.
items.reasoning: Technically strong contribution to spatial statistics combining several established tools (flows, amortization, sparsity) into a coherent scalable framework, but of specialized interest to the spatial statistics and Gaussian process community.

items.title: Activating the Annotator: Operationalising Lived Experience in Data Annotation
items.content: arXiv:2610.12701v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Perspectivist NLP has established that annotator positionality shapes labels for subjective tasks, but the field still lacks methods for operationalising it. Positionality is typically operationalised as a demographic form completed at recruitment: a static attribute recorded once and treated as a covariate, on the assumption that the knowledge it indexes is active when the annotator reads an item. This paper treats that assumption as a design problem and asks whether lived experience can instead be primed by the task itself. We introduce AXLE, a pre-annotation stage in which a scenario vignette anchors a short, axis-guided conversation that is synthesised into a first-person micro-narrative and returned to the annotator before labelling begins. In a 2x2 between-subjects study (104 annotators, 30 items, 1,040 annotations) on ambiguous hate speech spanning immigration, religion and gender, elicitation was associated with higher identity resonance and higher sensitivity to harm. It also increased label entropy and lowered inter-annotator agreement: the stage appears to surface plurality rather than manufacture consensus, which distinguishes it from annotator training, whose success criterion is convergence.

items.title: Evo$^2$: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution
items.content: arXiv:2610.13025v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Self-evolving agents are increasingly used to improve language model systems without human intervention through either weight updates or harness improvements. Existing approaches typically pursue these directions separately: some methods update model weights using self-generated experience, while others rewrite the harness that defines how an agent uses prompts, tools, context, and execution feedback. However, these approaches overlook the relationship between model weights and the agent harness. To connect these processes and ensure effective and smooth agent self-evolving, we propose Evo$^2$, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. For harness updates, we design a unified dual-role pipeline that a single policy serves as both a Proposer, which writes harness edits, and a Reflector, which diagnoses their effects and guides revision. For weight updates, harness modifications and their execution outcomes guide the training of both the Proposer and the Reflector. We further develop EvoTIDE, a training pipeline that recovers usable trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, then combines SFT with interleaved GRPO across the two roles. Extensive experiments across three coding benchmarks demonstrate that Evo$^2$ significantly outperforms existing self-evolution methods. It achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, compared with 62.6% and 41.0% for the strongest baseline, respectively. We also show that the evolved harnesses transfer to different tasks without further evolution and rank first in cross-benchmark evaluations. Our dual-role harness improvement framework is also able to extend to self-evolution with proprietary models, improving a GPT-5-mini agent's performance from 24.4% to 48.3%. These results demonstrate the applicability of the framework Evo$^2$ across domains and its broad transferability across models and tasks.

items.title: A Better Metric Will Not Save You: What You Compare Beats How You Compare It
items.content: arXiv:2610.13476v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Representational similarity measures (RSA, CKA, Procrustes) are chosen for the transformations they treat as irrelevant, and all of them take the set of conditions as given. That set is fixed by two decisions, which inputs are admitted and how they are grouped, both taken before the matrix a measure operates on exists: no invariance property reaches them. We measure what they are worth where the arrangement the conditions ought to have is known independently of the systems compared, the acoustic organisation of vowels, across fifteen languages and twenty-seven representations. Changing which categories are compared, at a fixed number of them, moves the gap between two representations by more than twice the effect being measured, while changing how many moves it not at all. In this setting rankings of models are identified under these choices, and rankings across languages are not.
items.author: Noureddine Khaous (LLF - UMR7110, UPCit\'e), Guillaume Wisniewski (LLF - UMR7110, UPCit\'e)
items.summary: Argues that representational similarity measures (RSA, CKA, Procrustes) are dominated by upstream decisions about which input conditions are compared and how they are grouped, rather than by the choice of metric. Using vowel acoustic organization across fifteen languages and twenty-seven representations, changing the compared categories moved the measured gap more than twice the effect being measured. A sharp methodological critique for interpretability and representational analysis.
items.reasoning: The finding that experimental design choices swamp metric choice has broad methodological implications for anyone using representational similarity analysis, including interpretability researchers; the empirical scope is solid though focused on a specific phonetic case study.

items.title: MVGraph: Benchmarking LVLMs on Evidence Composition across Multi-View Visual Graph
items.content: arXiv:2610.12961v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce MVGraph, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) on multi-graph reasoning where the evidence required by a query is distributed across multiple interrelated visual graph views. Although such evidence commonly resides in source-specific graphs, temporal snapshots, or local observations, existing graph reasoning benchmarks remain confined to a single self-contained structure, assessing only graph perception and reasoning while leaving the alignment and composition of evidence across views underexplored. MVGraph comprises 8k instances spanning 8 \textit{graph-theoretic} tasks, abstracted from two multi-graph scenarios (partial and temporal graph views). Each problem is programmatically constructed and verified to be unsolvable from a single view. Beyond end-to-end evaluation, we decompose multi-graph reasoning into four complementary capabilities---Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning---and design 29 diagnostic tasks with 64k instances to probe each one, along with golden intermediate representations for evaluating the intermediate process. Across 15 LVLMs, we reveal the difficulty of multi-graph reasoning and identify cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as prominent bottlenecks through stage-oriented diagnostics. Meanwhile, temporal constraints and increasing view counts expose further capability boundaries. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AAAndy-Zhu/MVGraph.

items.title: Multimodal Image-based Robotic Assistance and Guidance Environment (MIRAGE): A Novel Unified Framework for Surgical Navigation and Visualization
items.content: arXiv:2610.12780v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents the computational architecture and quantitative preclinical evaluation of MIRAGE, a multimodal image-guided robotic surgery framework for real-time visualization and navigation. It integrates stereovision scene reconstruction, augmented-reality (AR) video overlay, quantified heads-up display (HUD) navigation, and intraoperative ultrasound within the da Vinci console's TilePro display (Intuitive Surgical). Additional modules include optical/electromagnetic tracker registration, stereo calibration, fiducial rigid registration with RMSE feedback, and 3D point-cloud reconstruction. Video I/O and rendering run in a C++ backend, while a Python GUI coordinates calibration, registration, reconstruction, visualization, and user interaction through an in-process zero-copy binding layer. The framework formalizes spatial transforms, module states, and synchronization of heterogeneous video and tracking streams. Preoperative calibration uses synchronized checkerboard image pairs and optimization, with estimated intrinsics, extrinsics, and rectification reused intraoperatively. MIRAGE was validated in phantom experiments across da Vinci S, Si, Xi, and SP platforms. Across clinically relevant working distances, mean 3D reprojection error was 0.6mm, with best 0.1mm RMSE at 100mm on Xi. Results support MIRAGE as a preclinical technical-validation platform for accurate, responsive, and extensible multimodal surgical guidance.

items.title: PATACON: GPU-Parallel Tangent-Bundle RRT-Connect for Constrained Motion Planning
items.content: arXiv:2610.13195v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Fast whole-body motion planning enables continuous replanning for humanoid robots in dynamic environments while satisfying collision avoidance and kinematic constraints. However, constrained motion planning incurs substantial computational cost due to repeated constraint projection in addition to collision checking and nearest-neighbor search. Recently, GPU-based massively parallel planners have been proposed to reduce computational cost. Nevertheless, these planners still steer in the ambient configuration space, so projecting candidates that deviate from the manifold remains a significant source of overhead, particularly in highly constrained, high-dimensional problems. In this work, we introduce PATACON, a GPU-parallel bidirectional planner that explores tangent space to exploit the local manifold geometry induced by known constraint functions. Experiments on dual-arm closed-chain and humanoid whole-body constrained planning tasks show that PATACON outperforms the prior work as configuration-space dimension and constraint codimension grow, achieving up to an 11.25 times speedup. These results suggest that GPU-parallel tangent-space exploration brings constrained whole-body motion planning closer to real-time performance.
items.author: Gahyun Oh, Junho An, Suhyun Jeon, Suhan Park
items.summary: PATACON is a GPU-parallel bidirectional planner that steers directly on the tangent bundle of constraint manifolds rather than in the ambient configuration space, reducing the overhead of repeated constraint projection in highly constrained, high-dimensional planning. It targets fast whole-body motion planning for humanoids that must continuously replan in dynamic environments.
items.reasoning: A solid combination of two known ideas (massively parallel sampling-based planning and manifold-constrained steering) with a clear identification of where parallel planners lose time. Useful for humanoid whole-body control, but methodologically incremental over existing GPU-parallel planners.

items.title: Gaussian BROJA Partial Information Decomposition in Closed Form
items.content: arXiv:2610.13464v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The BROJA partial information decomposition provides an operationally motivated way to separate the information that two sources carry about a target into unique, redundant, and synergistic components. For continuous and high-dimensional variables, however, computing the BROJA decomposition requires solving a difficult optimization problem. Previous work showed that, when each source-target pair is jointly Gaussian, the problem can be reduced to finite-dimensional numerical optimization. Here, we derive a closed-form solution to this optimization problem, enabling direct computation of the BROJA decomposition in the general multivariate Gaussian setting. The resulting closed-form expression enables speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude for high-dimensional Gaussian BROJA PID. Code is available at https://github.com/brainsandmachines/Eigen_PID.

The Gaussian restriction limits scope, but the closed form and large speedups will be immediately useful in neuroscience and ML analysis.

items.title: Representation Alignment from a Few Paired Data via Distilled Optimal Transport
items.content: arXiv:2610.12781v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Aligning two independently pretrained unimodal encoders typically demands millions of paired examples. In this paper, we study the regime where only $N \sim 100$--$500$ pairs are available, while unpaired data on either side is abundant. Our method expresses every representation by its similarities to the $N$ paired anchors, which places both modalities in a common coordinate system; matches the two point clouds with a single entropic optimal transport problem solved over the entire pool, whose marginal constraints counteract the hubness that defeats nearest-neighbor matching; and distills the resulting plan into two lightweight encoders, so that the correspondence becomes inductive. We additionally put this marginal constraint in relation with the one-step hub corrections of the bilingual lexicon induction literature. Pairing is required only for the anchors: the unpaired collections may be drawn independently from the two marginals, so that no item outside the anchor set needs to have both of its modalities observed. We evaluate on image-text and molecule-text alignment, where our method outperforms existing approaches at the same anchor budget on Flickr30k, MS-COCO and ChEBI-20.

This drastically reduces the paired-data requirement compared to millions of examples. Valuable for data-scarce multimodal alignment, e.g., medical imaging.

items.title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty
items.content: arXiv:2610.13081v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.

items.title: A Step Harder, Not a Step Too Far: The Benefits and Limits of Curriculum Difficulty Progression in GRPO
items.content: arXiv:2610.13669v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Curriculum learning typically organizes training samples from easy to hard. In GRPO, medium-difficulty samples are attractive for online selection because they are more likely to yield informative group-relative learning signals, and prioritizing them can improve training efficiency. However, it remains unclear whether persistently selecting such samples also leads to the strongest final model performance, or whether training can benefit from progressing toward harder samples. Meanwhile, sample difficulty changes as the policy evolves, so fixed difficulty estimates can become misaligned with the current policy. We therefore re-estimate sample difficulty under the current policy and, inspired by the easy-to-hard principle of curriculum learning, design and evaluate a staged curriculum that progressively shifts the active difficulty band toward harder samples. Experiments on GSM8K show that persistent medium-difficulty selection does not achieve the strongest observed performance. Across three random seeds, progressing to a moderately harder difficulty band improves test accuracy to $0.6591 \pm 0.0077$, compared with $0.6449 \pm 0.0024$ for the fixed-medium curriculum. However, further progression to a harder difficulty band reduces accuracy to $0.6405 \pm 0.0053$. These results show that staged difficulty progression can outperform persistent medium-difficulty selection, but its benefit is non-monotonic. Effective GRPO curricula can therefore benefit from progressing beyond medium difficulty, while avoiding excessive progression toward overly difficult samples.}
items.author: Ronghan Li, Fei Chen, Mingyu Lu
items.summary: This paper studies whether GRPO training should persistently select medium-difficulty samples or progress toward harder ones, re-estimating sample difficulty under the current policy as it evolves. It provides an analysis of where curriculum difficulty progression helps and where it does not, refining the popular easy-to-hard heuristic for RL fine-tuning of reasoning models. The findings inform practical data selection in GRPO pipelines.
items.reasoning: Careful empirical study of a question many GRPO practitioners face, with the valuable insight that fixed difficulty estimates go stale as the policy evolves. Incremental in method but useful in guiding practice; importance depends on the robustness of the conclusions.

items.title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2610.13889v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.

items.title: Don't Guess, Just Ask: Evaluating Interactive Requirement Clarification for Repository-Level Software Development
items.content: arXiv:2610.13022v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As LLMs become increasingly capable of implementing software, a critical bottleneck emerges: whether they truly understand what users want. Users often begin with vague intent, leaving important requirements to be clarified through interaction. In repository-level development, misunderstandings can propagate and cause costly rework. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate implementation from complete specifications or underspecified requests, overlooking pre-coding requirement clarification. Prior clarification studies mainly focus on function-level tasks. It therefore remains unclear how well LLMs can transform vague intent into clear requirements through interaction and how this capability affects subsequent code generation.   We introduce ReqClarifyBench, an interactive requirement clarification benchmark for repository-level software development. It contains 341 tasks spanning game, miniapp, and web development, each with a vague user intent, a human-validated requirement document, and code evaluation artifacts. We employ LLM-based user simulators with diverse personas derived from real-world conversations. We evaluate six LLMs in terms of clarification effectiveness and generated requirement document quality. Results show that stronger clarification effectiveness does not necessarily translate into higher document quality, and performance varies substantially across user personas. We also find that coding-agent harnesses do not further improve requirement document quality compared with their base LLMs. These findings offer insights for building LLM-based end-to-end software development systems.

items.title: AudioTETRIS: Token Elimination via Transitional Importance Signals for Efficient Audio LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2610.13600v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. However, treating audio tokens as generic, isotropic features smooths over spectral transitions, destroying fine-grained phonetic transitions essential for decoding speech. In contrast, speech signals exhibit highly structured temporal patterns where information density peaks at acoustic transitions. We propose AudioTETRIS, a training-free, two-stage framework that uses the audio encoder's representation geometry as an acoustic prior for token importance before applying attention-based compression. Instead of discarding encoder structure after the encoding stage, AudioTETRIS propagates this prior directly into the LLM decoder to compute a per-token fused score. This score drives progressive top-$k$ token selection across decoder layers without requiring additional training or auxiliary models. Evaluated on Qwen2-Audio-7B, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, AudioTETRIS retains near-uncompressed performance on several speech tasks using only 25% of audio tokens, matches or surpasses full-token accuracy at moderate compression rates, and consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.

By preserving fine-grained phonetic transitions that coarse similarity-based methods destroy, it reduces the quadratic self-attention cost of audio token sequences without retraining.

items.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.13829v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source

It targets evaluation of recursive self-improvement claims in embodied agents.
items.reasoning: Addresses an important and timely evaluation gap in agent self-improvement research with a carefully designed controlled methodology. However, Minecraft-based benchmarks are crowded, the construction is complex (chains, probes, graph alignment), and real-world transfer of conclusions remains to be shown.

items.title: Primal-Dual Flow Matching for Sample-Wise Constrained Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.12699v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We consider the problem of learning to generate data while satisfying a prescribed \emph{sample-wise} constraint with a user-specified probability of constraint satisfaction. Starting with a population-level constrained negative log-likelihood minimization and using a flow-matching (FM) parameterization, under regularity assumptions and sufficient expressivity of the velocity field family, we derive guarantees on the probability of constraint satisfaction for the corresponding primal-dual optimization algorithm. We provide a practical implementation of this approach, called Primal-Dual Flow Matching (PDFM), which has direct control over constraint satisfaction rate and requires only binary membership oracle feedback for constraint satisfaction, avoiding the need for differentiable distances, projections, or special structure of the constraint set, such as convexity. We show that PDFM improves constraint satisfaction over vanilla FM and achieves competitive performance against constraint-aware baselines while maintaining distributional fidelity. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZhengyanHuan/PDFM.
items.author: Zhengyan Huan, Peter Y. Lu, Shuchin Aeron
items.summary: PDFM extends flow matching to generation under sample-wise constraints with a user-specified probability of satisfaction, deriving theoretical guarantees for a primal-dual optimization algorithm. The practical implementation requires only binary membership oracle feedback and offers direct control over the constraint satisfaction rate.
items.reasoning: Controlled constrained generation is important for scientific and safety-critical applications, and sample-wise (rather than population-level) constraints with explicit satisfaction-rate control is a distinct contribution. The theory-to-practice bridge is promising, but significance depends on how well it scales versus constraint-projection alternatives.

items.title: Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization: Unified Learning from Offline Demonstrations and On- and Off-Policy Rollouts via a Shared Regression Target
items.content: arXiv:2610.12830v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reasoning post-training draws on offline demonstrations and policy-generated rollouts, yet conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) separates their objectives and limits continued reuse of collected responses. We propose \textbf{Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization} (CBPO), which makes these sources compatible with one regression loss through a fixed-reference target. Because the generating policy does not enter this target, positive and negative offline completions, reference responses, and current and historical rollouts can share a common reward-labeled record format and replay buffer. As new responses enter the buffer, optimization retains the same regression objective without coordinating separate SFT and RL objectives or requiring stored behavior-policy probabilities, importance weighting, or a learned critic. Restricting the available sources gives offline, on-policy, and off-policy variants, while CBPO-Unified combines them. Across two model scales and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CBPO delivers leading \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} performance across benchmarks and data regimes. On Qwen3-1.7B, CBPO-Unified improves benchmark-averaged \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} over SFT DAPO by 2.33 and 4.44 percentage points, respectively. In the replay ablation, retaining historical rollouts improves these metrics by 1.87 and 3.72 percentage points over the no-history configuration.
items.author: Du Cheng, Junyu Lu, Jingfan Zhang, Yuzhuo Zhang, Haoxuan Jia, Shichao Weng
items.summary: CBPO unifies supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning for reasoning post-training through a single regression loss with a fixed-reference target that is independent of the generating policy. This lets offline demonstrations, reference responses, and current and historical rollouts share a common reward-labeled replay buffer, enabling continued reuse of collected responses without coordinating separate objectives.
items.reasoning: The SFT-then-RL pipeline inefficiency is a real problem in reasoning post-training, and a unified off-policy-compatible objective that reuses all data sources is attractive and timely. The framing is compelling, but whether the single regression target matches the performance of well-tuned hybrid pipelines needs strong empirical support.

items.title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
items.content: arXiv:2610.13073v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.

items.summary: The paper studies why fixed-size memories fail to keep distant information usable as context grows, examining large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identifying failures in single-step writes that accumulate interference. Double-Take proposes improvements to capacity, binding, and selectivity as distinct requirements for usable long-context memory. This contributes to the architectural frontier of sub-quadratic long-context models.

items.title: PDE-PFN: Prior-Data Fitted Neural PDE Solver
items.content: arXiv:2610.13334v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Motivated by the success of large language models (LLMs) with broad generalizability and robustness to noisy or unreliable pre-training data, we explore in-context prediction of PDE solution fields using approximate pre-training data. In addition, inspired by the posterior predictive mean-based inference mechanism of the in-context learning in prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), we propose PDE-PFN, a prior-data fitted neural solver that approximates the posterior predictive mean of PDE solutions via in-context learning. PDE-PFN builds on a PFN architecture with self- and cross-attention mechanisms of Transformer and is pre-trained on noisy approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks, serving as diverse but not necessarily exact priors. Through experiments on a range of two-dimensional PDEs, we demonstrate that PDE-PFN achieves empirical generalization across heterogeneous equations, robustness under noisy priors, and zero-gradient-update in-context inference capability. PDE-PFN achieves competitive or improved predictive accuracy relative to the evaluated baselines while supporting flexible context and query representations.

Inspired by LLM robustness to noisy pre-training data, it approximates the posterior predictive mean of PDE solutions via transformer-based self- and cross-attention. This allows solving PDEs without exact simulation data.

items.title: Randomized Momentum Transport with Cheap Predictors
items.content: arXiv:2610.13789v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Momentum methods such as STORM and second-order momentum track the gradient by adding a transport correction to momentum, at the cost of an extra oracle call per iteration. We introduce randomized momentum transport, which evaluates the correction with probability $q$ and otherwise uses a cheap prediction, with importance weighting that preserves the conditional mean and adds $(q^{-1}-1)$ times the prediction loss to the variance. Under transport-bias, second-moment, and residual-control assumptions, linear minimization oracle (LMO) updates, including normalized, sign, and exact spectral (Muon) directions, retain an $O(T^{-1/3})$ stationarity bound for each fixed $q>0$ with a single-gradient initialization. For unnormalized STORM, some $q<1$ lowers the leading coefficient of our sufficient gradient budget if and only if the gradient-difference noise modulus exceeds the smoothness constant, by at most about $10\%$. An online diagonal predictor admits a regret-to-convergence guarantee. At approximately equal oracle cost, querying a quarter of the corrections lowers the final training loss by $18$ to $43\%$ on MNIST1D and raises the test accuracy of Hessian-vector transport on CIFAR-10 by $1.5$ points.

items.summary: This paper randomizes the transport correction in momentum methods like STORM, evaluating it only with probability q and otherwise using a cheap prediction with importance weighting. Under stated assumptions, linear minimization oracle updates including normalized, sign, and Muon-style spectral directions retain O(T^-1/3) stationarity bounds with reduced per-iteration cost.
items.reasoning: Timely theory given rising interest in Muon-style optimizers, showing principled cost savings with preserved rates; solid optimization theory, but impact depends on empirical adoption of the randomized scheme.

items.title: Golden Anchor for Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.13217v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Video generation supports digital content creation, with applications in virtual avatars, AI-driven filmmaking, interactive game engines, and world models. State-of-the-art systems achieve controllability primarily through image-to-video (I2V) generation, in which an injected anchor image determines the identity, composition, and style of the resulting video. In modern pipelines, this anchor is synthesized by a text-to-image (T2I) generator. This raises a largely overlooked question: Are images obtained directly from the T2I model truly suitable for current video models? Our analysis shows that anchor aesthetic and quality scores are weakly correlated with downstream video quality. The structure-and-texture score is negatively correlated with I2V video quality in both the visual and motion dimensions. Fine-tuning the T2I model on an image reward accordingly yields anchors with visibly denser structural and character detail: they score higher on image metrics, yet lower the video reward on every I2V model we test and change downstream motion unpredictably. items.title: From 2.1M Hours of Raw Broadcast Audio to Finnish Speech SSL: Confidence Filtering and Architectural Analysis at Scale
items.content: arXiv:2610.13102v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Broadcast archives offer scale and diversity for self-supervised learning (SSL) but contain substantial noisy, non-speech, and multilingual content. Prior work typically relies on voice activity detection or language identification (LID) to extract speech, ensuring presence rather than quality. Whether and how to filter unlabeled speech by quality for SSL, particularly from noisy broadcasts, remains underexplored. We present a large-scale Finnish SSL study starting from 2.1M hours of unconstrained broadcast audio. We propose automatic speech recognition (ASR) confidence as a proxy for pretraining data quality and show 3-7% relative WER improvements over LID-based filtering despite a smaller training set. We further address the lack of controlled architectural comparisons in speech SSL by evaluating Transformer, Macaron-Net, Conformer, and E-Branchformer at matched parameter budgets. Our models improve upon prior Finnish SSL baselines, particularly at Base scale and out-of-domain.

items.title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.12914v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.

It addresses a real weakness of imitation-trained robot policies. Relevant to making robot manipulation policies robust and recoverable.

items.title: VETR: Execution-Grounded Self-Improving Agent for Symbolic Graphics Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.13098v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.

items.title: Competence-Aware Orchestration for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: arXiv:2610.13144v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing complex reasoning through role specialization and collaboration, yet a key challenge remains: how can collaboration be adapted to a backbone's competence on the current query? This problem matters because more collaboration is not always better--richer coordination may help on difficult cases, but it also incurs additional token cost and redundant interactions. We propose a two-stage competence-aware framework for automatic MAS orchestration. It first models the LLM backbone's task-conditioned competence for the current query, and then uses this signal to adapt role activation and the communication graph. Across six benchmarks, our method achieves an average score of 93.81%. Experiments with six LLM backbones of varying competence levels further show that our method adjusts collaboration according to the inferred competence: for higher-competence backbones, it improves average accuracy from 87.22 to 89.97 while reducing token cost by 36.26%; for lower-competence backbones, it yields a further average gain of 4.58 points over existing methods. The same trend also holds on unseen backbones.

items.title: Local Diagnostics of Learned Event Representations for Anomaly Detection at the HL-LHC
items.content: arXiv:2610.13437v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Anomaly detection, the identification of collision events that deviate from Standard Model expectations, is one of the most promising model-agnostic strategies for new-physics searches at the Large Hadron Collider. Searching for rare events in learned low-dimensional representations removes the need to commit to hand-crafted observables a priori, but sacrifices the immediate physical interpretation those observables provide. For anomaly detection to enter a discovery pipeline, flagged events must therefore be diagnosed locally, both to distinguish potential new physics from mismodeling or detector effects and to identify observables for targeted follow-up searches. We evaluate supervised and self-supervised neural embedding strategies on COLLIDE-2V, a 750-million-event dataset simulated under realistic High-Luminosity LHC conditions, using the reconstruction error of an autoencoder trained in the learned latent space as the anomaly score. Across the configurations and benchmark signals considered, supervised objectives, which exploit simulation process labels during training, generally outperform their self-supervised counterparts and, in their best configurations, improve on an autoencoder trained directly on kinematic features, raising the signal efficiency at 10% background acceptance on all held-out processes. We further introduce a local diagnostic pipeline that fits a Gaussian Mixture Model to the SM latent space, profiles each component through high-level observables without process labels, localizes the flagged events, and ranks observables by their local discriminating power. The ranking recovers the defining kinematics of the held-out processes, while correlating the anomaly score with the same observables quantifies how closely the score tracks them, revealing cases where the most discriminating observable is not the one the score follows most closely.
items.author: Donatella Genovese, Philip Ploner, Simone Scardapane, Stefano Giagu, Thea Klaeboe Aarrestad
items.summary: This paper addresses the interpretability gap in using learned neural embeddings for anomaly detection at the LHC, where flagged events must be diagnosed to separate new physics from detector mismodeling. It evaluates supervised and self-supervised embedding strategies and provides local diagnostics to recover physical observables from learned representations. This work supports deploying anomaly detection into actual discovery pipelines at HL-LHC.

items.title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2610.13521v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) by routing domain-specific data to specialized teachers, integrating their capabilities through dense token-level supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, domain routing only distinguishes the supervision sources for different domains; updates from all domains still act on shared parameters. When teachers differ substantially in response style and domain expertise, supervision that is effective in isolation may still lead to persistent gradient conflicts and capability degradation during joint optimization. To address this challenge, we propose Cross-Teacher Guarding for MOPD (Road MOPD), which introduces non-routed teachers as auxiliary cross-domain critics on the same student trajectories and coordinates multi-teacher supervision through token-level credit assignment and gradient updates. Specifically, cross-teacher-guided credit assignment uses teacher agreement to strengthen token-level corrections jointly supported by the teachers and attenuate conflicting signals; preventive multi-teacher gradient projection uses auxiliary gradients from the same trajectories to constrain potentially conflicting updates and adaptively controls projection strength to retain target-domain learning signals. In experiments, Road MOPD mitigates degradation in the disadvantaged domain, gains over 5 percentage points under high conflict, and improves overall performance in low-conflict and three-domain settings.

It introduces non-routed teachers as auxiliary cross-domain guards during joint optimization to prevent capability degradation. This addresses a real obstacle to scaling multi-teacher distillation.

items.title: Cancerous Backdoor Attack: Gradual Activation via Invisible Tokens and A Stage Controller
items.content: arXiv:2610.12644v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Backdoor Attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) typically follow a trigger-response pattern, where satisfying a trigger condition activates a single terminal behavior. However, this single-point backdoor activation does not explore attacks in which malicious behavior develops gradually through multiple intermediate stages before reaching the terminal activation stage. We present Cancerous Backdoor Attack, that gradually corrupts an LLM's reasoning over a sequence of interactions by leveraging invisible tokens and a stage controller. Specifically, invisible tokens provide hidden stages to the model without appearing in the user's visible request and the stage controller tracks the attack's progression during inference to realize gradual activation. We evaluate Cancerous Backdoor Attack across several reasoning datasets. The attack consistently produces gradual reasoning corruption across models and tasks. We compare Cancerous Backdoor Attack with prior backdoor attack baselines to demonstrate our proposed attack outperforms the baselines. Our results indicate that reasoning corruption can develop gradually before it becomes visible, making answer accuracy alone insufficient for detecting backdoor attacks.

This advances understanding of stealthy, staged threats against deployed language models.
